# New blog

*Active Objection, 2026-04-07* · [Original post](https://activeobjection.substack.com/p/new-blog)[^original-post]

Welcome to my new blog. I’m a nearly 75-year-old Quaker male living in the Midwest.

The idea of ACTIVE OBJECTION came to me when I was reminded that we are cautioned to not resist evil. Although there have been numerous times when I did just that, I have become convinced that responding to evil diverts our attention and energy away from creating constructive ways to address injustice.

# War Has Changed

*Active Objection, 2026-04-07* · [Original post](https://activeobjection.substack.com/p/war-has-changed)[^original-post]

### **We utterly deny all systems of violence and war**

*Wars are conducted in significantly different ways today. **Artificial intelligence** systems select targets, too often incorrectly. Armed, unmanned drones operated remotely kill the people targeted, largely eliminating the need for human soldiers on the ground. Large numbers of civilian men, women and children are killed or maimed. Civilian infrastructure has become targets despite that being a war crime.*

*Ironically, those with relatively small armed forces have successfully used drones against countries with great military might.*

*The new machines of war require different forms of human interaction, such as software developers, engineers and remote control drone pilots. New groups of people who might conscientiously object to doing this work.*

*Historically military **conscription** was used to force people to fight. Today there is an **economic draft**. Students with huge loans, people who require jobs that provide health care, and those who are impoverished and can find no jobs are **conscripted** into work which they may **conscientiously object** to doing. Peacemakers need to offer guidance and support.*

*We continue to utterly deny all systems of violence and war.*

Jeff Kisling (a Quaker)

# Why we must embrace Indigenous leadership

*Active Objection, 2026-04-11* · [Original post](https://activeobjection.substack.com/p/why-we-must-embrace-indigenous-leadership)[^original-post]

I’m preparing to go to Iowa City again to participate, for the third time, in a work camp at the Great Plains Action Society’s (GPAS) Indigenous-led Urban Resilience Hub.

It’s a three hour trip each way to the Hub from where I live in Madison, Wisconsin, and that is difficult since I lived most of my life without a car for environmental reasons. But that is one sign of how important I believe it is for me to show up.

It’s important for me to continue to deepen relationships with my native friends and others who are helping to build this Hub. It is a continuation of many years along this spiritual path for me.

I am led by the Spirit to acknowledge the harm Quakers did when we settled on this land. And the tragedy of the forced assimilation of native children at the Indian residential schools. Healing can’t begin until the damage has been named and acknowledged, and apologies offered. I have spoken with each of my Indigenous friends about Quakers and the Indian residential schools.

The most significant hurdle I continue to face as I ask Quakers to embrace the concepts of LANDBACK, Mutual Aid, and abolition are why non-native people must embrace Indigenous leadership, and what the implications of LANDBACK are for non-natives. I have trouble convincing others that, for our own spiritual integrity, we must stop participating in the current system of injustice, i.e. colonial capitalism.

> “It has become clear to some of us who are called Friends that the colonial capitalist economic system and white supremacy are contrary to the Spirit and we must find a better way. **We conscientiously object to capitalism and white supremacy.**” — Epistle to Friends Regarding Community, Mutual Aid and LANDBACK

As the existential environmental catastrophe is accelerating before our eyes, the question is how to slow down the ongoing damage and how to begin to repair Mother Earth.

Indigenous peoples of this land have been living through collapse for over 500 years. They are living continuations of knowledge systems, such as traditional ecological knowledge (TEK), that predate capitalism by thousands of years. Centering Indigenous leadership means following this traditional ecological knowledge (TEK).

**Non-native people should be immensely grateful when that knowledge is shared with us.**

> *“This hub is a reclamation of Indigenous agency that will help the community work towards environmental and social justice. Essentially this is a true testament to Indigenous Futurism.”* **— GPAS Iowa City Urban Resilience and Innovation Hub**

Quakers insist that we are led by the Spirit, and that will not change. But that does not preclude following the leadership of others. Quakers aren’t being asked to surrender this fundamental principle of our faith. But we also desperately need the wisdom of Indigenous peoples.

We must represent Indigenous voices authentically — there’s a real risk of speaking **about** rather than **with**. By partnering with the Great Plains Action Society our work, our decolonial work, is Indigenous led.

Another way for non-native people to support GPAS is by participating in the [Decolonial Repair Network (DRN)](https://www.honornativelandfund.org/decolonialrepairnetwork) because DRN functions with input from the GPAS, i.e. it is indigenous-led. And the funds raised are for GPAS.

---

**Intercommunalism: What Showing Up Actually Means**

Intercommunalism is the practice of building networks between communities that share resources, knowledge, and power horizontally. It is distinguished from charity (which flows downward) and allyship (which supports from a distance).

> ***Intercommunalism requires co-presence: showing up in the same spaces, sharing the same risks, doing the same work.***

The developing relationship between Midwest Quaker communities and GPAS demonstrates a natural intercommunal relationship. Quakers bring institutional resources — meetinghouses, networks, legal and financial literacy — that GPAS currently needs to build the Hub. GPAS brings Indigenous leadership, including TEK, working models of decolonial infrastructure, and rootedness in frontline community.

---

#### Self-abnegation

The most common failure of ally-ship is the substitution of presence for participation: attending a meeting, signing a statement, making a small donation, and returning to life unchanged. What is needed instead is institutional self-abnegation — redirecting the meeting's endowments, properties, and institutional energy toward the actual work of repair.

Supporting the Hub calls for Quakers to be present on site, or to participate remotely at times when we are invited to do so. These work camps are an invitation.

The Great Plains Action Society has an active calendar of events you can follow on their Facebook page.

# Be an Accomplice

*Active Objection, 2026-04-17* · [Original post](https://activeobjection.substack.com/p/be-an-accomplice)[^original-post]

I spent the past few days at the Great Plains Action Society’s Urban Resilience Hub in downtown Iowa City. This was the third time GPAS has invited us to come to help actually build the Hub. I was able to come every time.

Being at the Hub again shows the difference between an ally and an accomplice.

An **ally** expresses support, often from safety. They attend the panel, pass the minute, update their language, make a donation, share the link. Allyship is largely **self-referential** — it is about the ally’s identity, growth, and stated values. It is conditional: the ally can step back when things become costly. The risk stays low. The relationship remains on the ally’s terms.

**An accomplice takes on risk alongside those in the struggle.** The term, popularized in a 2014 essay by Indigenous Action Media called “Accomplices Not Allies: Abolishing the Ally Industrial Complex,” describes someone who puts their body, their resources, and their privilege into the work in ways that create real exposure — who follows the lead of those most affected rather than advocating for them from outside, and who disrupts systems rather than merely witnessing them.

The core difference: an ally stands *beside* the struggle. An accomplice stands *inside* it, with consequences.

Quakers have a long history of what might be called sanctuary practice: hiding escaped enslaved people, supporting conscientious objectors, accompanying undocumented immigrants. The Resilience Hub is a twenty-first century expression of that same logic — a space designed to be a refuge, a resource, and a site of community power for people the dominant culture has marginalized.

Iowa Friends have the opportunity to be part of building that space in its formative period.

# Learn, unlearn, and wrestle with hard topics

*Active Objection, 2026-04-18* · [Original post](https://activeobjection.substack.com/p/learn-unlearn-and-wrestle-with-hard)[^original-post]

> [![May be a graphic of text](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Bf9K!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F154ffdde-b13d-4137-9ee5-94a54099bcec_1200x628.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Bf9K!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F154ffdde-b13d-4137-9ee5-94a54099bcec_1200x628.jpeg)
>
> *If we’re going to talk about change in this country, we need to stop tiptoeing around the truth. It’s time to name the real issues - the messy ones, the painful ones, the ones that shape our relationships, our communities, and our futures.*
>
> *We’re creating a space where people can **learn, unlearn, and wrestle with hard topics**, while practicing what it means to hold space for one another with **honesty and care.***
>
> **Community conversations, Great Plains Action Society**

---

#### My Quaker perspective

I agree, ***we need to stop tiptoeing around the truth*****.**

My entire life has been rooted in Quaker communities and practices. As I was coming of age I was confronted with a choice that would set the course for the rest of my life. The issue was how I would respond to the requirement that every male in this country must register for with the Selective Service System, the draft. For me, this was in 1969, as the war in Vietnam was raging, and the country was in turmoil. The war was deeply unpopular and young people were demonstrating across the country.

I was blessed to have the support of Quakers who lived the truth that we must work for peace, which often created problems for us with the status quo in this country. Many Quakers were led to actions that put them at risk for prosecution. I was led to non-cooperation with draft by turning in my draft cards. I expected to be arrested, but was not.

I have never judged others who applied for conscientious objector status, which allowed them to fulfill their military obligations by doing two years of civilian service.

But, if I were to stop tiptoeing around the truth, I would say alternative service was a ploy by the military, which was successful, to deal with those who objected to war.

I hadn’t thought about it this way before, but this is an example of the difference between being an ally versus being an accomplice. An **ally** expresses support, often from safety. An **accomplice** takes on risk alongside those in the struggle. Which usually requires being physically present with those in the struggle.

Conscientious objection to the draft is like being an **ally** for peace. Draft resistance is being an **accomplice** for peace.

#### What is the truth?

I can only strive to be attentive to the truth the Spirit is trying to reveal to me. Following are the pieces of the truth as I’ve been led to understand them. This ongoing process has involved **learning, unlearning and wrestling with hard topics.**

My ancestors came as settler-colonists to the rural Bear Creek community. They engaged in mutual aid as they shared equipment and labor among their farms. Some were accomplices in the underground railroad network, placing themselves at risk. Many worked in various ways for peace.

One major piece of our Quaker story, though, is about the Quaker involvement in the forced assimilation of native children. This is one of the most painful things I’ve had to learn, unlearn and wrestle with. This was so important because it set the context for Quakers and our relationships with Indigenous peoples from then on. How could Quakers say we believe there is that of God in everyone while at the same time working to erase the culture of Indigenous peoples?

Over the years since there have been some efforts by Quakers to bring attention to this tragedy. Unfortunately, these efforts come within the context of the ongoing Christian, colonial capitalist violence against Indigenous peoples. Very few Quakers today understand the depths of the ongoing intergenerational trauma and how that continues.

One of the things I’ve had to unlearn is that the capitalist economic system worked well. Until very recently, capitalism had worked for those who are considered white in this country. But it never really did for everyone else. It is morally wrong to require capital to obtain essentials like food, shelter and healthcare when so many people had little or no money, through no fault of their own.

When non-native people try to help Indigenous people, they almost always do so from within the colonial capitalist mindset, the very systems that continue to oppress. The collapse of our current economic and political systems means white people are now also experiencing what is like to live when they don’t have enough capital.

These are some of the things I’ve had to learn, unlearn and wrestle with:

1. What Christian, colonial, capitalist violence is.
2. Work for peace and justice must dismantle capitalism and colonialism.
3. Just communities are grounded in mutual aid.
4. Just communities are based upon thousands of years of Indigenous wisdom and ways.
5. We must be physically present in communities working for justice. We must expose ourselves to the risks oppressed folks face.
6. Too often Quakers are allies.
7. We must become accomplices, instead.

It has been a blessing for me to experience what this can look like, during the times I’ve been led to join the work at the Great Plains Action Society’s Indigenous-led Urban Resilience and Innovation Hub.

This is a model I hope Friends will work to replicate in our communities.

The question I have been sitting with is what keeps going wrong? Every time I try to explain what I am learning and doing related to my work with the Great Plains Action Society with my Quaker meeting, conflict always results. This is ironic because the meeting has a long history of good work with Indigenous peoples.

As others have tried to tell me, there is a large gap between the meeting and the extensive work and experiences I’ve been led to over the past decade.

This led to a spiritual crisis last December during which I could not attend meeting for several months. A care committee for me was helpful, and I returned to the meeting.

At Sunday’s meeting I had been led to ask for a donation from the meeting to the Great Plains Action Society where I had been going to work on their new Urban Resilience Hub. Some Friends were upset and the request was denied.

I need to find a way to bridge this disconnect. I mentioned the possibility of forming a working group for this purpose and some interest in that was expressed. But it would be better to form a Clearness committee so that the questions about the meeting’s relationships with Indigenous peoples can be clarified.

There are many aspects of this to be explored, and different Friends might focus on different parts. One part could be an exploration of the documents in the recently opened safe, for example. We could also explore the book, This is the Route of our Forefathers.

I believe Bear Creek meeting can continue to be an example of Quaker engagement with Indigenous peoples.

The reasons I’ve begun to write by hand again are to slow myself down and to break my usual patterns of using the computer to write.

I am led to this need to slow down in part because I am alienating the very people who are so important to me, and to my spiritual life.

When I wrote about my Quaker meeting declining my request for funds I realized the real issue was that I had not been sharing enough with the meeting for them to understand why I believed this is an opportunity for the meeting to engage with Indigenous people.

My Quaker meeting, that I and generations of my family going back to 1871, have attended. George and Deborah Standing and George and their five sons, Henry, George, Charles, Alfred, and Josiah purchased eighty acres of land for $5.00 per acre.

A lot happened in the 155 years since. Quakers from this meeting (Bear Creek) have contributed a great deal to the Quaker and the wider communities.

Many perspectives, both Quaker and that of the wider world have changed over time since then.

My spiritual leadings lately have been related to Quaker’s relations with Indigenous people. Bear Creek Friends has a unique history of much good work. I believe we can build on that.

The major areas of concern are settler-colonialism and the forced assimilation of native children. I have made the mistake of making people defensive about these things, which has created significant barriers with the meeting today.

I am working on praying about ways I can change that. This slowing myself down by handwriting is a step on this journey.

# Journal 4/23/2026

*Indigenous Leadership*

*Active Objection, 2026-04-23* · [Original post](https://activeobjection.substack.com/p/journal-4232026)[^original-post]

One of the most significant barriers I have found with my vision for Quakers relates to centering Indigenous voices and the puzzling objection that Quakers strive to always be led by the Spirit. The implication being that we should not be led by Indigenous people.

I find that to be offensive on multiple levels. Do we think Indigenous people would ever suggest anything contrary to the Spirit? To think so must come from not knowing any Indigenous people.

And do we believe Quakers would ever act against the leadings of the Spirit?

I need to raise this now because the Spirit has convinced me that it is crucial to seek Indigenous leadership from the very beginning of any work on a new path forward.

There are many reasons why.

Non-native people must recon with the theft of native land and the horrors of the forced assimilation of native children.

Non-native people have raped Mother Earth. To the extent of environmental catastrophe. Indigenous people have vast stores of knowledge and experience of how to live in harmony with our environment and each other. Indigenous peoples have for centuries demonstrated how to live peaceably.

We are in desperate need of that knowledge now.

# Journal 4/24/2026

*The story of my interest in Native Americans*

*Active Objection, 2026-04-24* · [Original post](https://activeobjection.substack.com/p/journal-4242026)[^original-post]

What is the story of my interest in Native Americans?

My interest began from my spiritual leadings as a Quaker youth. Being raised on farms in Iowa, I felt a connection with the land. And I fell in love with the mountains we camped in for many years.

When I moved to Indianapolis in the early 1970’s, I was horrified by the filthy air. This was before catalytic converters were installed in cars, which hid the visible exhaust, but didn’t stop the greenhouse gas emissions. I had a profound spiritual experience of visualizing my beloved mountains hidden in clouds of smog. That vision was tied to this photo of Long’s Peak that I had taken and developed. That vision, when I was in my early twenties, had profound impacts on the course of my life.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!xeiR!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F5927a290-01c7-4de0-b405-0b4e9d46b191_2000x1519.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!xeiR!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F5927a290-01c7-4de0-b405-0b4e9d46b191_2000x1519.jpeg)

Long’s Peak, Rocky Mountain Park, Colorado © Jeff Kisling

One was that led me to live without a car. There were many consequences from that. It determined what I bought at the grocery store, because I had to be able to carry it all on the walk home.

I became a life-long runner. And I began to carry my camera with me everywhere, so I would be in a position to see more of the world I was walking through and could take the photos since I wasn’t trapped inside a car zooming past all of this.

People became aware of this witness without me saying anything about it. I thought it gave me some moral authority when I did speak of my concerns about our environment. One article I had published was titled **Cars as Weapons of Mass Destruction**. These things were the subject of my daily blog posts.

These concerns about Mother Earth led to my connections with Native Americas, which I plan to expand upon later.

Another consequence of this was my deep disappointment that very few other Quakers refused to be part of modern society’s fossil fuel addiction.

It is occasionally suggested that I have a romanticized view of Indigenous peoples. I say, instead, that I see people who live in a manner consistent with how I have been led to live, in ways that honor and protect Mother Earth.

That is why I am so grateful for the opportunity to help build the Great Plains Action Society’s Urban Resilience Hub in Iowa City.

# Journal  4/25/2026

*Indigenous Lives Matter*

*Active Objection, 2026-04-25* · [Original post](https://activeobjection.substack.com/p/journal-4252026)[^original-post]

I am grateful that some Quakers have responded to what I’ve been writing about my experiences with Indigenous people.

Concerns have been raised regarding the concept of centering Indigenous voices. There is fear that is not compatible with the foundation of Quaker faith, which is to follow leadings of the Spirit. Which is not the case.

I’m reminded of objections I heard when holding a sign that said **Quakers Know Black Lives Matter**. People passing by sometimes said, **I thought all lives matter**. The reason for saying Black Lives Matter was to counter repeated evidence that Black lives in this country did not matter, because of the violence against them.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Lz_a!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb64b7bc5-9b57-452e-b11c-f25b73e196a3_191x346.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Lz_a!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb64b7bc5-9b57-452e-b11c-f25b73e196a3_191x346.jpeg)

Similarly, to me, centering Indigenous leadership is saying **Indigenous Lives Matter.** This is especially tragic due to the epidemic of **Missing and Murdered Indigenous Relatives.**

Of course this work occurs in the context of the history of Friends’ impact on Indigenous peoples in this land.

As we focus on leadings of the Spirit we might consider through whom has the Spirit spoken to Quakers in the past? John Woolman’s ministry against slavery came from his experiences among enslaved people. I have spent the past decade among Indigenous people.

It has always been frustrating that there have been so few ways for Friends to be present with Native Americans. The invitation to Friends to be involved with the Great Plains Action Society’s Indigenous-led Urban Resilience and Innovation Hub in Iowa city is a way for that to happen.

This is a concrete example of centering Indigenous voices.

At this time things aren’t ready for visitors. But when that time comes, I encourage Friends to visit the Hub.

> “All actions require the guidance of the Indigenous Peoples involved and need to be done with respect, cooperation, and ongoing consultation.... We acknowledge that part of our journey is to decolonize our own thinking and sit in the discomfort and pain of confronting where we need to deepen our understanding, bear witness, and transform our behaviour.”
>

# Journal  4/26/2026

*Active Objection, 2026-04-26* · [Original post](https://activeobjection.substack.com/p/journal-4262026)[^original-post]

I have been singularly unable to convince Quakers living in the country that we are unfaithful as long as we remain comfortable living in this country’s ongoing colonial capitalism.

We have been warned about materialism being the seeds of war by George Fox, John Woolman, and Martin Luther King.

This country has become a war machine at home and abroad. We suffer tremendous moral injury from the relentless violence being done in our name. But that doesn’t compare to the death and violence others suffer as a result.

Peacemaking and justice can not happen from within these systems of injustice.

We are wasting time and resources when we advocate to restore democracy, because democracy as defined here is the vehicle of injustice, war and death.

Faithfulness requires us to leave these systems.

That is done by building alternative systems of peace and justice:

* Mutual Aid
* LANDBACK
* Abolition of police and prisons, replaced with community safety and care

Until we change, we remain complicit.

# Journal 4/27/2026

*Evils of Capitalism*

*Active Objection, 2026-04-27* · [Original post](https://activeobjection.substack.com/p/journal-4272026)[^original-post]

I often write about the evils of capitalism, but I am realizing I haven’t written much about what the alternatives might look like. Before I give examples from my own life, I need to explain the concept of the **economic draft.**

The economic draft represents the idea that although the military draft stopped being active, for now, people are still being conscripted into the capitalist economy.

Young men from economically oppressed communities often join the military because of lack of other sources of employment. They also enlist to help advance their education without taking on huge student load debt.

In the general public, students who incur large student loans are forced into high paying jobs that often don’t reflect their values.

Similarly, many are forced to take on any work that provides health insurance.

#### Capitalism

* is founded on the labor of enslaved people and land stolen from Indigenous people
* is increasingly violently enforced by militarized police and soldiers
* transfers wealth to the wealthy, impoverishing the rest of us
* creates poverty and homelessness
* has caused and continues to cause environmental catastrophe
* is the root cause of war

It looks like I’ll need a new post to continue with examples of rejecting capitalism from my life

# Journal 4/28/2026

*Christian, colonial, capitalist violence (CCV)*

*Active Objection, 2026-04-28* · [Original post](https://activeobjection.substack.com/p/journal-4282026)[^original-post]

When I asked my friend Ronnie James, of Des Moines Mutual Aid, why many people are unable to see the injustices of capitalism, he said they hadn’t experienced life without enough money to live comfortably (yet). Those who struggle are quite familiar with the many consequences of lack of money.

In this country the economic system is one piece of three interlocking systems referred to as **Christian colonial capitalist violence (CCV).**

**Christian** in this case is not condemning the Christian religion-just the justifications provided by such things as the Doctrine of Discovery, that gave European explorers permission to claim ownership of land not already claimed by Christians, and subjugate the Indigenous peoples there.

**Colonial** refers to settler-colonists who dispossessed Indigenous people’s land and culture.

**Capitalism** refers to a system that commodifies resources and the labor of people for profit.

The fusion of these three is why these unjust systems have persisted and why they are so resistant to change, because they support each other. Attempts to address capitalism are challenged by certain mainstream religious arguments, these days from White Christian Nationalists, for example.

The colonial part resists any attempts to return Indigenous sovereignty and land.

**Extraction** of natural resources and human labor are the main components of colonial capitalism today. I recently wrote about the **economic draft**, various mechanisms that force people to stay in situations that don’t reflect their values. That make it very difficult to find work that promotes justice and real community care.

# Journal 4/29/2026

*New conscientious objector and active objection*

*Active Objection, 2026-04-29* · [Original post](https://activeobjection.substack.com/p/journal-4292026)[^original-post]

Who doesn’t feel like their life is out of control today?

It is hard to watch the impacts on those we care about. We feel deep moral injury as we witness the global harms to people and to Mother Earth from this country’s political and economic systems.

I began this new journal to share what I have learned about what is going on, and what our responses might be.

I have been led to see the political and economic systems developed by the White men of wealth are the basis of most of the problems we are living through now. Those systems were built on stolen land, and the labor of enslaved people.

The collapse of these systems is now on full display, domestically and globally.

Unfortunately, I see so many people who want to address this collapse are working to try to fix the current systems, when we should be working to build alternatives based upon justice.

I was led to the concept of the **New Conscientious Objector** (NewCO) when thinking about how we could object to these systems of injustice we are embedded in.

It feels like we are facing a modern **draft**. Being **conscripted** into these unjust systems. That made me think about **draft resistance** (as I did during the Vietnam War). But I was reminded of **resist not evil.** I believe that is a crucial concept—to NOT waste time and energy engaging with evil. We should be building just alternatives instead. That led to the concept I call **active objection**, the title and focus of this journal.

# Working with different communities or cultures

*Active Objection, 2026-05-02* · [Original post](https://activeobjection.substack.com/p/working-with-different-communities)[^original-post]

These days I often wonder whether the accelerating collapse of our political and economic systems will overwhelm us before we can make the changes I advocate for.

That is all the more reason to begin or continue to work on building alternatives now. To implement mutual aid, LANDBACK, and the abolition of police and prisons. Other reasons are that these political and economic systems are fundamentally unjust and need to be replaced.

One thing that concerns me, that I have witnessed many times, are the inappropriate and destructive ways white people act when they try to engage with oppressed communities.

When white people would ask me how to support communities suffering injustice, I would tell them to **just show up** at events organized by these communities. Very few people show up to these events which take a lot of effort to put on.

By saying **just show up** I meant to attend. I also meant by **JUST** attend to mean don’t do anything else until you are invited to do so. Which will likely not happen at your first engagement. Some level of trust must be built, first. That will involve demonstrating your commitment by continuing to show up and in an appropriate manner.

This highlights the difference between an ally and an accomplice. An ally offers support from a distance. An accomplice shows up, repeatedly, including accepting risks of doing so.

This message from my friend Sikowis Nobiss, founder of the Great Plains Action Society, demonstrates what happens when people do engage appropriately. Importantly, we were **invited** into this work.

Sikowis shared this with those of us who spent a week doing construction at the new Indigenous-led Urban Resilience and Innovation Hub in downtown Iowa City recently.

# Introduction to Practitioner-bridge

*Active Objection, 2026-05-03* · [Original post](https://activeobjection.substack.com/p/introduction-to-practitioner-bridge)[^original-post]

I have caused a lot of disruption in my Quaker meeting over the past several years, much to my dismay. The root of these conflicts is the significant gap created as a result of my past decade of work in Indigenous communities.

This was puzzling to me because the meeting has supported the Prairie Awakening/Prairie Awoke ceremony for many years. This is an Indigenous-led event held just a few miles from the meetinghouse.

Recently I have come to see there is another gap there. One couple in the meeting was deeply involved in the ongoing planning of Prairie Awakening. They have develop deep relationships with the Indigenous people involved. Many others in the Quaker meeting have attended this annual event, but don’t have such relationships.

That couple has served as a bridge between their Indigenous friends and the Quaker meeting. I recently discovered there is a concept referred to as a practitioner-bridge, which describes a person who bridges such gaps.

Learning about practitioner-bridges has already been very helpful to me. It has taught me a different perspective regarding this gap between my Quaker meeting and me. # Expanded role for the Decolonial Repair Network

*Active Objection, 2026-05-05* · [Original post](https://activeobjection.substack.com/p/expanded-role-for-the-decolonial)[^original-post]

Note: This has not yet been discussed by the Decolonial Repair Network. As I often do, I write to help think through things.

As I’ve been thinking more about the awesome Great Plains Action Society’s (GPAS) Indigenous-led Urban Resilience Hub in Iowa City, I’ve become concerned about the impact on the Hub’s staff as interest in the project grows.

The Decolonial Repair Network that I am part of was formed specifically to support GPAS. We hold monthly calls to talk about work being done by members of the network and by GPAS. And we raise money for GPAS.

The monthly calls involve education related to decolonization. But it is a slow and fragmented process.

The most important thing allies must learn is how to interact appropriately in Indigenous spaces.

It finally occurred to me that a program I was involved in years ago in Indianapolis is a perfect fit for this.

The program is the Quaker Social Change Ministry (QSCM) from the American Friends Service Committee (AFSC). Despite the name, people who are not people of faith will not find much religious content in the program.

QSCM was designed to help Quaker meetings engage with an oppressed community near the meetinghouse. Most of QSCM is about how to engage with such communities before connecting with them. The key concept is accompaniment, which means taking direction from the community. That requires deep listening and refraining from offering suggestions until input is requested by the community.

QSCM proved to be highly successful when the Quaker meeting I attended in Indianapolis (North Meadow Circle of Friends) formed a long term relationship with the nearby Kheprw Institute, a Black youth mentoring community.

I’ll tell stories about what happened in the next post.

Indigenous ways worked for centuries. This traditional knowledge can help us heal Mother Earth and our broken communities.

*Active Objection, 2026-05-30* · [Original post](https://activeobjection.substack.com/p/my-story-begins)[^original-post]

This is the first post of what will be a series of articles about my life as a Quaker activist. Until recently I wrote nearly every day on a variety of topics. But it feels like I need to organize all of that into a comprehensive narrative of what I have done and learned over the 75 years that I’ve lived thus far. I am a white male, aware of the pervasive white supremacy of this country’s mainstream culture.

I believe many young people today have a better understanding of the implications of this than my generation does. Young people know about Black Lives Matter, settler colonialism, environmental, economic and political collapse and the rapid rise of authoritarianism. And are morally exhausted by the extreme violence and intentional genocide this country is perpetrating globally and domestically.

I hope some of what I have experienced and learned might be useful to those who want to work toward justice for all now.

To begin, I should explain why this blog is called **Active Objection**. It had been common to talk about resistance to injustice. But resistance is reactive, and diverts energy, time and resources to resistance, resources that should be used to build just alternatives, instead. Authoritarianism is built on rapidly creating innumerable situations whose purpose is to keep us off-balance and demoralized.

Active objection means stating our objection to an injustice, but then to actively work for just alternatives. The intent of this blog is to explore what some of these alternatives are, and how to build them. # Walk Cheerfully Over the World

*Active Objection, 2026-05-31* · [Original post](https://activeobjection.substack.com/p/walk-cheerfully-over-the-world)[^original-post]

How did I arrive at this point in my life’s story?

I was born in Bangor, Maine, in 1951. My parents both grew up in the rural Iowa area of Bear Creek, near Earlham, Iowa. Shortly after their high school graduation, they married, and then moved to Bangor because Dad had enlisted as a military policeman, this being the time of the Korean War. They must have had some interesting conversations, because Quakers strongly oppose militarism, and Mom was raised in a multi-generational Quaker family (Standing). They hadn’t had much time to get to know each other and their beliefs. They were married at the Bear Creek Quaker meeting in 1950. They had a double wedding there, with Mom’s best friend Lucky, who married Wolf Guindon. Shortly after, Lucky and Wolf moved to Costa Rica where they joined other Quakers who settled in Monteverde. They established Monteverde Friends School which also taught local, non-Quaker students. They developed hydroelectric power from a stream and a cheese factory.

Dad soon became a member of Bear Creek meeting and joined Mom in working with many Quaker organizations and causes. Dad was instrumental in raising more than one million dollars for the restoration of the headquarters of the Friends Committee on National Legislation (FCNL), directly across from the Hart Senate Office building in Washington, DC. After FCNL’s Executive Secretary, Joe Volk, spent several days traveling around Iowa with Dad, fundraising for the renovation, Joe ask if there was anyone in Iowa that Dad didn’t know.

Scattergood Friends School has played a significant part in the lives of my family, and in mine. This co-ed Quaker boarding high school and farm are owned and operated by Iowa Yearly Meeting (Conservative), which is the umbrella organization for about a dozen Quaker meetings in the Midwest, including Bear Creek Meeting.

It is important to explain that the word ‘conservative’ means maintaining (conserving) traditional Quaker practices. These practices are rooted in the concept that the Spirit or God can guide us today, as it has always done. This worship is referred to as ‘unprogrammed’ because it involves sitting together in silence for about an hour, rather than having a planned program with a minister, signing hymns, etc.

Worshipping together sometimes leads someone to speak into the silence if they hear a spiritual message. Anyone can give such a message. On a given Sunday several people might be led to speak. Other times no one does.

It is important to explain that Quaker worship is not confined to this hour of worship on Sunday mornings. We believe we should listen for spiritual guidance always.

Be patterns, be examples in all countries, places, islands, nations, wherever you come, that your carriage and life may preach among all sorts of people, and to them. Then you will come to walk cheerfully over the world, answering that of God in everyone; whereby in them ye may be a blessing and make the witness of God in them to bless you.

(Quaker) George Fox 1656

# What if I had known?

*Active Objection, 2026-06-03* · [Original post](https://activeobjection.substack.com/p/what-if-i-had-known)[^original-post]

I left things up in the air at the end of yesterday’s post, ”**why am I reading my journals now?”**

I’m reading to refresh my memory of those times. And sharing what my journals looked like then. A young person today might relate to what I was going through at that age.

But I am also looking at my formative years across the span of my life experiences since. A persistent question sits in my mind and spirit that asks, **“what if I had known?”**

What if I had been taught an accurate understanding of settler colonialism? Of the Quaker involvement in the Indian residential schools? About the stolen land our homes, meetinghouses, Scattergood Friends School and Farm were built on, and continue to occupy?

What if I had been taught about the fundamental injustices of the capitalist economic system?

I’m not asking these questions now to make white people feel guilty. I ask them in sorrow of what could have been. I would have started my life from a truer spiritual place.
 Jeff Kisling

I’m not sure what to think about why I wasn’t taught about settler-colonialism and the institutions of forced assimilation while attending Scattergood in the late 1960s. I don’t think teachers were told not to teach these things. I believe they were uninformed themselves.

And yet, as a young adult, I sensed an unease the one time I remember the subject coming up. It was said of the member of our meeting that she went to help the native children. I think many Quakers held that opinion. I would believe, tragically, many still do.

For whatever reason, this history didn’t reach us as students at Scattergood then.

I have been spending time at Scattergood recently related to working on the Great Plains Action Society’s Indigenous-led Urban Resilience Hub in downtown Iowa City, which has had all kinds of consequences for me. One is that from conversations with students and staff, I know colonialism is discussed in classes at Scattergood now.

Another is that I had the opportunity to talk at a community meeting with the students about the Hub during one of the times I was participating in a work week at the Hub. Scattergood is making various connections with the Hub, including providing housing for some of those who come to work at the Hub.

This return to my journals and my early days at Scattergood was initially focused on my significant struggles related to the draft (Selective Service System). But I’m looking at all of that now with an understanding of colonial capitalism.

I’m thinking of how powerful it would have been if we understood our relationships to the land we walked over during the peace march to Iowa City when I was a student there in 1969.

And during the climate march from Scattergood into Iowa City in 2013. I was able to participate in that march, too. I put photos and video together to make this video of the Earth Walk/Climate March.

# Synthesis: Spiritual Formation + Justice Work

*Threads connecting Scattergood (1969) and Iowa City (2016)*

*Active Objection, 2026-06-04* · [Original post](https://activeobjection.substack.com/p/synthesis-spiritual-formation-justice)[^original-post]

I had hoped to write a clear account of my life story. I had envisioned a linear timeline, but that isn’t how the story is unfolding. There are so many interconnected threads.

**Synthesis** is depicted as the combination of **spiritual formation** and **justice work**. That’s how life developed for me, the spirit and justice work informed each other.

The left margin of this diagram is labeled **Quaker formation runs through every layer.** The right margin says **relation to land deepens across time**. That characterization about land surprised me, at first. But it shows what I’ve been learning from my Indigenous friends. That our relationships with the land are the basis of everything.

---

The direct paths from Scattergood (1969-1970) to Now are:

* Conscientious Objection -> Active Objection

  * Scattergood gave conscientious objection grounding. Vietnam taught its limits.
* The Missing Map -> This Writing Project

  * What Scattergood did not teach (Meskwaki land, Quaker complicity) became the central wound and central question of all my writing 55 years later.
* Quaker Practice -> Theological Framework for Repair

  * Silent worship, the Inner Light, “that of God in every person”. Internalized at Scattergood. Became the theological argument that settler colonialism is incompatible with Quaker faith.
* Walking the Land -> Walking as Spiritual Practice

  * Running and photography at Scattergood - embodied attention to the land. Prefigured the 94-mile First Nation-Farmer as a prayer and the Urban Resilience Hub as labor.
* Community of Integrity -> Standard for Mutual Aid

  * The Scattergood community modeled integrity-based living. That standard exposed charity as insufficient and demanded solidarity.

# The Throughlines

*It's not about me*

*Active Objection, 2026-06-05* · [Original post](https://activeobjection.substack.com/p/the-throughlines)[^original-post]

I really don’t like calling attention to myself. But mine is the only story I know. As early Quakers said, we should let our lives speak. That is what I’ve tried to do, at times in better ways than others. I have truly made some bad mistakes, some of which I will be writing about.

I’ve been blessed to have been led to many wonderful experiences. Many of which were terrifying to contemplate, but led to some of the best parts of my journey.

Spirituality is difficult to write about because we just don’t have the words to express it. When I say I was led to do something, that means that I’ve had a spiritual message to do it. Quakers believe everyone is given spiritual leadings, because we believe there is that of God or the spirit in every person. But many people don’t recognize it when the spirit speaks to them. Or they may get a sense of such a leading, but do not follow it. Often following a leading requires some sacrifice. Sometimes significant risk.

Sometimes early Quakers were referred to as “publishers of the truth”, meaning they spoke in public, or published what they wrote about their beliefs. I have this funny picture in my mind of Quakers in those days writing blog posts. It is remarkable that we can press a button that will put our writing on the internet for all the world to see, even if usually very few people actually read the post.

Another reason I believe I’ve been led to write is because I sense a deep spiritual poverty in this country, and the world. I hope some of what I write might help others, spiritually.

The systems we could once depend upon for our basic needs are rapidly collapsing. Many of us who once lived comfortably in our socioeconomic status are now joining those who have always struggled.

Years ago, when I asked my good friend Ronnie James, as we worked together at Des Moines Mutual Aid, why more people are not aware of the fundamental injustices of the capitalist economic system, he said it was because they personally hadn’t been adversely affected by capitalism, yet. Now, more and more of us are feeling the pain.

The political and judicial systems in this country can no longer be used for positive change because they are so corrupt. For almost eighty years the Friends Committee on National Legislation (FCNL) served well as a Quaker voice in Washington, DC. Those efforts worked when Congress was receptive to the needs and concerns of their constituents. That is no longer the case, as huge sums of money now drive political decisions. Part of what I’ve learned is we should no longer be trying to reform these systems. You cannot create change if you remain embedded in the unjust systems you are trying to change.

The other major throughline of my life has been to learn about, and participate in the lives and work of oppressed communities, including the Kheprw Institute, a Black youth mentoring community in Indianapolis. I witnessed some of the racism they had to deal with. And, more recently, I’ve been led to multiple ways and occasions to get to know and work with some Indigenous people in this country and Canada. In part because, as an environmentalist, I appreciate the sustainable ways they’ve always lived.

**Now, some of these century old ways are needed by all of us in order to survive the collapse.**

As a Quaker, I’ve learned more and more about Friends’ involvement in the theft of native land, the generational wealth from the land, and the Indian residential schools. Institutions of forced assimilation of native children. Now I take every opportunity to support and work with my native friends. Most recently by going to the Indigenous-led Urban Resilience and Innovation Hub which is on an acre of land in downtown Iowa City.

I’m also writing because I’m seeing how important it is for Quakers to address our complicity in settler-colonialism, and learn how we can return to many of the Indigenous ways of living and surviving in communities under oppressive conditions. The Hub is a concrete example of how this can be done now. Resilience Hubs are not limited to urban areas, or only Indigenous communities. I envision a resilience hub being built at my rural Quaker meeting. These are basically survival systems.

Looking back, there are six threads that run through all of this. What follows in this series will keep returning to these six throughlines

1. Spiritual formation and leadings (Quaker practice)
2. How my journey has come full circle, back to Scattergood Friends School, the Quaker boarding high school I attended
3. Challenging unjust systems rather than reforming them
4. Learning from and working alongside Black communities (Kheprw Institute)
5. Learning from and working with Indigenous communities (GPAS, the Hub)
6. Quaker complicity in settler colonialism — and repair

# My spiritual leading in the moment

*"He listened"*

*Active Objection, 2026-06-06* · [Original post](https://activeobjection.substack.com/p/my-spiritual-leading-in-the-moment)[^original-post]

Yesterday when I wrote about the Spirit and leadings, I kept thinking of one particular adventure that illustrates these concepts.

I remember one of the most significant leadings of my life, which happened at my first meeting with the Kheprw Institute in Indianapolis. Where I met people who would become close friends.

Below is a blog post I wrote about that meeting. But this was all unknown territory that rainy night. As explained below, it took a little persistence to make the meeting happen at all. But one aspect of a spiritual leading is that it won’t let you go until you deal with it. Or choose to ignore it.

I had to ride my bicycle to where we were meeting because I refused to own a car for environmental reasons. And my connection to the Kheprw Institute came from an environment event as explained below. That I lived close enough that I could bicycle is because I lived in inner city Indianapolis, only two miles from Kheprw. The socioeconomic levels of both neighborhoods were similar but the racial demographic was different, with KI being in a Black inner city neighborhood. After my first two years in Indianapolis, when I was part of the Friends Volunteer Service Mission, which was in another lower economic class neighborhood, I looked for housing in similar areas thereafter. This was part of my anti-capitalism.

I attended North Meadow Circle of Friends, an unprogrammed Quaker meeting just a few blocks from where I was living. The proximity of the meetinghouse to the Kheprw Institute (KI) was significant because I helped the meeting adopt the new program from the American Friends Service Committee (AFSC) called Quaker Social Change Ministry, that was intended to get Quakers out of their meetinghouses and into the surrounding community. North Meadow Friends engaged with the program, and the Kheprw Institute was the community organization we partnered with. Some of us rode our bicycles to KI after Quaker meeting, to join the monthly book discussions at KI.

It was hard to leave these friends when I returned to Iowa, but the connections didn’t end. For example, although I lived without a car in Indianapolis, one of my godson’s had a car that he could no longer use. So we donated that car to KI. When I was leaving for Iowa, I left kitchen utensils, pots and pans, and some clothing with KI.

At my mother’s Zoom memorial some ten years later, Miss Fair, one of the KI leaders, spoke during the service, saying she didn’t know my mother, but she knew me, and had seen how I paid attention to the spirit. She said, “he listened.” And that was a reflection of how I had been raised.

Following is a blog post I wrote about that initial Kheprw Institute experience.

---

## Kheprw Institute

The path the Inner Light led me down related to racism started about four years ago (circa 2012). I was deeply involved in the environmental activist movement, mainly through the Keystone Pledge of Resistance. At that time various environmental groups would organize national days of education or action to try to raise awareness about our environmental crisis. These things were organized via the Internet. When I learned of an upcoming day of action, I looked to see where something in Indiana was occurring, and the only event was at a place I’d never heard of, the Kheprw Institute (KI). I was led to attend that event. I found an old building that had previously been a convenience store in an inner-city neighborhood in Indianapolis. But it was full of young, black kids enthusiastically showing us their aquaponics system and rain barrel making enterprise as ways they were working for the environment.

I was intrigued, and wanted to learn more. They did have a web page, but the only contact information was an email address. On the web page I saw one of their projects was “Open Source Activism”, to develop computer applications to support activism. Being a computer programmer, I thought this would be the way for me to connect with KI.

I sent an email message indicating that I would like to be involved with that, but did not receive a reply. I was thinking this was not meant to be, but this was one of those times when the Inner Light was not going to let me give up, so after a couple of weeks, I sent another email message. After some time, I received an offer to meet at KI. I arrived on my bicycle on a dark, rainy evening, to find the same group of about a dozen kids in their early to late teens, and KI’s leaders, Imhotep, Pambana, Miss Fair, and Alvin.

After some greetings, we all sat down, and I thought we would talk about programming languages and projects. Instead everyone looked at me, and Imhotep said, “Tell us about yourself.” I talked a little about being concerned about the environment and working with the Keystone Pledge of Resistance, and my work at Riley Children’s Hospital. “Tell us some more.” So I mentioned I was a Quaker, and Miss Fair enthusiastically talked about Quakers and the Underground Railroad. When she stopped, everyone looked at me. I said something along the lines of how grateful I was that my ancestors had done that work, but Quakers try to not take credit for things they personally hadn’t done.

Which led me to talk more about how Quakers didn’t see religion as something only involving listening to a sermon once a week, and left me at the point where I needed to provide an example from my own life. Since KI is built on concern for the environment, I spoke of how I had reluctantly purchased a used car for $50 when I moved to Indianapolis, mainly for trips home to Iowa. Car rental was not common in the early 1970’s. When my car was totaled several years after that, I decided to see if I could live in the city without a car, and have since then. I was hoping that would show how Quakers try to translate what they believe, what they feel God is telling them, into how they actually live their lives. At that point Imhotep, with a smile on his face, said something like “Thirty years? You are a warrior.” I had never been called a warrior before. It seeming a humorous term to use for a pacifist, (and I suspect that was his intention now that I know him better) but I liked it.

I have since learned that Imhotep is very good at drawing stories out of people. So again, he said, “OK, tell us some more.” I finally realized, and realized I should have anticipated, that this was more an interview to see if I was going to fit in, and the usual surface information wasn’t going to be adequate.

*I remember everyone looking expectantly at me and wondering what to I should say next. I also clearly remember the Inner Light telling me what I needed to do. I turned to each person and said “Quakers believe there is that of God in everyone, and that includes you, and you…” The very first time, I think I hesitated slightly as I was asking myself, “OK, we Friends always say this, but do you really believe this of a group that is different from you?” And I’m really glad the answer was an immediate and emphatic YES, but it also seemed to reaffirm that by exploring it intentionally. At that point I remember smiling at the thought, and the young person whose eyes I was looking into saw it, too, I think. Each person smiled at me as I said that to them, and I had the impression they were thinking, “of course”. I strongly felt the presence of the Spirit among us.*

That finally seemed to satisfy the questioning. This was a real revelation to me, how it is important to express spiritual matters as well as you are able when the situation calls for it. (It is also important NOT to do so when the situation does not call for it.) And to be alert for those possibilities, and how the Inner Light guided me through that evening. That set the tone for my involvement with KI since that night, for which I am profoundly grateful.

**[Presencing: Case Study by Jeff Kisling, Unflinching, Jul 17, 2024](https://unflinching.blog/2024/07/17/presencing-case-study/)**

# What does Active Objection mean?

*Resist not evil*

*Active Objection, 2026-06-07* · [Original post](https://activeobjection.substack.com/p/what-does-active-objection-mean)[^original-post]

What does **active objection** mean? Why is it the title of this blog?

This is what I wrote on the [introduction to this website/substack](https://activeobjection.substack.com/p/new-blog) page.

> *The idea of **ACTIVE OBJECTION** came to me when I was reminded that we are cautioned to **not resist evil**. Although there have been numerous times when I did just that, I have become convinced that responding to evil diverts our attention and energy away from creating constructive ways to address injustice.
> **—Jeff Kisling***

Active objection grew out of my years thinking about conscientious objection, and my eventual decision that even that framework was insufficient,

At some point the thought came to me that I conscientiously objected to our current systems of **Christian, colonial, capitalist violence**, which is the way oppressed communities define it.

During the Vietnam War, all 18-year-old males were required to register with the Selective Service and faced being drafted into military service. One alternative was to register as a **conscientious objector**, doing two years of community service instead.

I had from the beginning realized that I could not agree to be a conscientious objector, because to do so was a way to deflect criticism away from the draft and conscription. I knew I should resist the draft completely, and I eventually did. The only reason it took so long to do this was to give my family more time to be comfortable with my choice. They wanted me to do alternative service as a conscientious objector, because they didn’t want me to face the possibility of a felony conviction and imprisonment if I resisted the draft. In the end I was not arrested.

> *The time we spend ‘resisting evil’ could be better spent in trying to find out where we can do better ourselves. You do not change others by opposing them—rather, by respecting and trying to understand and learn from them, you can both benefit and move nearer the truth. A life of example—showing the possibilities and fruits of a life lived in love and concern for others, is the only way to overcome evil.*
>
> *I do not want my example to be alliance with evil. Thus, I cannot serve with the Selective Service System. However, I will not set myself against it. I will break my ties with Selective Service, and concentrate on the difficult task of working for peace in whatever way I can.*
>
> **—from the letter to my draft board, February, 1972.**

---

(Quaker) Marshall Massey, a member of my Quaker yearly meeting, Iowa Yearly Meeting (Conservative) recently wrote:

> Friends who have been in conversation with me, these past two years, have heard me speak my objections to the idea of “**resistance**”. We are forbidden to resist evil — an absolute, unqualified prohibition! — by the historical Jesus (Matthew 5:39), and I think many of us are also feeling that same teaching from the Christ in our hearts and consciences.
> **—Marshall Massey**

Active objection does not resist evil. Instead, it names and acknowledges the injustice, but then the focus is on building better, more just communities and alternatives.

Rather than opposing these systems, active objection works to build what should replace them — mutual aid networks, LANDBACK, community-based safety and care. Even something as small as the Friends Committee on National Legislation's **"War Is Not The Answer"** button I wear on my camera strap is part of that: a daily reminder of what we're building toward.

# What was the real story behind my draft decision?

*Active Objection, 2026-06-09* · [Original post](https://activeobjection.substack.com/p/what-was-the-real-story-behind-my)[^original-post]

I’m working on becoming a better writer, and I’m disappointed in my recent post. I didn’t say some things because I didn’t want hurt anyone. And I was uncomfortable writing about the intense emotions that were generated in myself and others, my parents in particular.

There was a lot of fear regarding my decision to turn in my draft card, in several different ways. I was afraid at the thought of being arrested and imprisoned. And I had a very naive idea of prison or I would have been more scared. Maybe not have gone through with the draft resistance? I don’t know.

**I clearly saw the spiritual damage I would suffer for the rest of my life if I didn’t act according to my beliefs.**

I was most afraid of not measuring up to the principles that other Quakers had been faithful to. There was a strong, multigenerational history in my Quaker community of men and their families doing what they were led to do regardless of the consequences. Many of these examples came at significant cost. Some were imprisoned. Conviction would result in a felony record. Which often makes it much more difficult or impossible to be hired for many jobs. Some **left the country** because of this, and developed a Quaker community in Monteverde, Costa Rica.

I saw how highly regarded these people were as examples of how Quakers should put their faith into action. Their example extended far beyond their draft decisions, because these were the very people Quakers looked to from that point on to provide leadership in all kinds of ways.

I wanted my life to be such an example, too. But one of the things I remember struggling with the most was that I should not base my own draft decision as way to get some of that respect. To not do the ‘right’ thing for the ‘wrong’ reason.

My greatest surprise was how upset my parents were during this whole process. I expected them to be worried, but not the depth of emotion these discussions generated. I was shocked that they were so forceful in pressuring me to take the safe route of doing alternative service. While I was trying to figure all this out, as a backup plan I did apply for, and was granted conscientious objector status.

I was allowed to leave Scattergood School for a few days after my eighteenth birthday, when all males in the country were required to register for the draft. The idea was to have more time to discuss this with my parents. We didn’t make much progress.

This turned out to be the most difficult part of my decision to return my draft card. I felt betrayed by this. All my life I had heard stories of, and witnessed myself, the many ways Quakers put their beliefs into practice. My parents supported all of that.

My time at home was drawing to a close. I felt I needed to act on my decision then, while I was in Marshalltown, where the draft board was located.

It was a cold winter day when I walked to the draft board. I stood out in the cold for a while, trying to work up the will to go inside. Eventually I did. The clerk was very kind, asking me if I was sure I was sure of my decision, asking if I wasn’t still in high school? I didn’t express my thought that thousands of other young men were being conscripted at the very same age.

Looking back on this, it seems a bit humorous that I turned in my draft card TWICE. Because, when I returned home and told what I had done, my parents were extremely upset. They asked if they could have more time to process all of this. So I wrote to the draft board and asked them if they would give me more time, and they sent my draft card back to me. I think they were relieved they wouldn’t have to deal with this, after all.

After several more months, my parents realized I wasn’t going to change my mind. But the time had allowed them to do more thinking and they didn’t stand in the way of me turning in my draft card a second time. Which I did.

---

### Letter to Bear Creek Monthly Meeting 1972

Homer Moffitt, Clerk
Bear Creek Monthly Meeting

Dear Friends,

I am thankful for your kind letters and encouragement concerning my work in Indianapolis. I am learning much about love, and as I respond to the love of others, and they to mine, we are all amazed at how it grows.

I am enclosing a statement I have written concerning conscription, and my decision not to cooperate with the Selective Service System any more. I sent a copy of that statement, along with my draft cards, to my draft board.

Again, I tried very hard to follow the leading of the inner light. If I alone were making the decision, this would probably not be my choice. Thomas a’ Beckett, torn between his obligations to the Church and those to the State, was searching for guidance. When he realized all the forces that influence him—selfish desires for power and personal gain, fear of punishment or displeasing people, etc., he said. “I am loathsome.” But then he heard what he believed to be the voice of God saying, “Nevertheless, I love.”

I, too, feel shamed when I realize the factors that often influence my decisions and actions. On this matter, I have tried very hard to be sensitive to the will of God, and hope to do so in the times to come. Still somewhat uncertain that my choice is right, I am comforted in knowing that He still loves.

Love,
Jeff Kisling

---

**In reply:**

Dear Jeff,

We have found your statement explaining your relationship to the Selective Service System very moving. Several of us are aware that your decision on this has been a difficult and lonely one. We want to assure you of our love and support as you meet the events which result from your courageous stand.

*On behalf of the Peace Committee of Bear Creek Monthly Meeting*

# Why didn't I know?

*Active Objection, 2026-06-15* · [Original post](https://activeobjection.substack.com/p/why-didnt-i-know)[^original-post]

When I become frustrated that Quakers are not more knowledgeable and concerned about our settler colonization of this land, I remind myself that I was ignorant of much of this until a short time ago (around **2017**).

#### I did not know. Looking back now, I wonder **WHY** I didn’t know.

---

#### tom kunesh’s challenge

tom kunesh, an Indigenous Quaker, wrote about this in **2022**.

> *I have been looking for a sign that quakers in the USA recognized and opposed the oppression that comes with colonialism. All indications prior to 2010 are to the contrary: as settlers originating from Europe, quakers enjoyed the military peace and occupation of Turtle Island by England and other european nations. “Friends” profited from colonial expropriation of indigenous people’s land and resources.*
>
> kunesh, tom (2022) “Decolonizing Quaker Moves to Innocence: What Would it Take to Decolonize the “Quaker Peace Testimony”?,” Quaker Religious Thought: Vol. 139, Article 5. Available at: <https://digitalcommons.georgefox.edu/qrt/vol139/iss1/5>

---

#### Entirely Different Boarding Schools

I found it ironic when I realized the Quaker boarding high school I graduated from in **1970**, Scattergood Friends School and Farm, was established (**1890**), at **the same time** Quakers and others were involved in establishing some of the Indian boarding schools.

Both were **residential institutions** designed to mold young people in specific ways. For Quakers, the goal was to help students grow in their understanding of Quakers and our role in the world. This was sometimes referred to as a “guarded” education intended to minimize the broader, secular culture’s influence on us. Based, in fact, on developing critical thinking skills to serve as the tools to resist such assimilation for the rest of our lives.

This is then head of school, Thomas Weber, introducing Paula Palmer’s talk about the Quaker Indian Boarding Schools, at Scattergood Friends (boarding) School, July, **2019**.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!zM4G!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F860097ae-4afb-4111-957d-43dd580a9964_3000x1213.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!zM4G!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F860097ae-4afb-4111-957d-43dd580a9964_3000x1213.jpeg)

#### Indian Boarding Schools

The **opposite** was true of the Indian boarding schools, as they were referred to. The goal was **forced assimilation** into the encroaching culture of the European settlers. The goal, according to Captain Richard Henry Pratt's speech (in **1892**) in which he used the now well-known phrase to describe his philosophy of assimilation was: **"Kill the Indian in him, and save the man."**

It is horrific that native children were torn away from their families. Many subsequently died from disease brought by the settlers, from exposure when they tried to escape, or from physical abuse. These schools were often hundreds of miles away from their tribe.

The reported discovery of children's remains found in May, 2021, at the Kamloops residential school in British Columbia, provoked a widespread international outcry. And investigations at other residential schools.

In the summer of **2017** my Quaker yearly meeting, Iowa Yearly Meeting (Conservative) held a panel discussion about building bridges with Native peoples. This was first time I heard **Sikowis (Christine) Nobiss** speak. Over the intervening years we’ve done a lot of work together, me in a supporting role. And our friendship has grown.

#### First Nation-Farmer Climate Unity March

In **2018** we were both part of the **[First Nation-Farmer Climate Unity March](https://firstnationfarmer.com/)** that she organized with Ed Fallon. The purpose was for a small group of Native and non-Native people to spend eight days walking and camping together from Des Moines to Fort Dodge, Iowa, ninety-four miles, along the path of the Dakota Access Pipeline. The intention was for the group to get to know each other by sharing stories as we walked. That worked brilliantly, and various combinations of us have worked on many things together since.

At that time I was profoundly ignorant about settler-colonialism and the Indian boarding schools. I remember wondering how that history affected the Native people I was walking with. Perhaps my most ignorant thought was wondering whether the Native people on the march knew this history. Whether they had personally been affected. Knew of the Quaker involvement. Would they be judging me because of this history? Should I bring it up? Apologize?

Sadly, I am now very familiar with the deep multigenerational trauma that every Native person in this land and Canada lives with even now.

#### Why Didn’t I Know?

I didn’t know about this earlier, because no one taught me. As tom kunesh said above, there was silence from Quakers about this.

# Lingering Issues

*Tension with my Quaker meeting*

*Active Objection, 2026-06-18* · [Original post](https://activeobjection.substack.com/p/lingering-issues)[^original-post]

Yesterday, I wrote that I asked myself, “Who is this person? And what is he being led to do with the weight of this knowledge and concern?”

I am seventy-five-year-old white male Quaker, and I am still evolving.

#### Indianapolis

I spent my adult life in Indianapolis, doing research in infant lung development at Indiana University Medical Center. Outside of work, I was involved in environmental and social justice issues. In particular, living without a car, which was possible because of public transportation in Indianapolis. That impacted every day of my life, from getting to work, to the grocery store, to my godson’s baseball practice and games.

#### Retirement to Iowa

One of the most difficult things I was confronted with when I retired and moved to Iowa in 2017, was the lack of public transportation, which meant I had to use the family car on occasion. That really hurt because it felt like I was no longer being faithful to my environmental leadings.

The most significant changes came from opportunities to work with Native people, specifically with Ronnie James at Des Moines Mutual Aid and Sikowis Nobiss, founder of the Great Plains Action Society (GPAS).

That knowledge grew — learning about present-day Native struggles, Quaker settler-colonialism, and Quaker involvement in the Indian Boarding Schools.

That knowledge also changed the answer to “what was I being led to do with the weight of this knowledge and concern?”

On a personal level, I became involved in the Decolonial Repair Network that supports the work of the GPAS. And I was able to attend the four work weeks at the Indigenous-led Urban Resilience Hub being built by GPAS in Iowa City.

It was the disconnect between this concrete example of Indigenous-led work and the problems getting my Quaker meeting to support it that triggered my spiritual crisis. I believe Quakers need to confront historical relationships with Indigenous peoples, and engage when we are offered an Indigenous invitation to help repair the damage.

That was the reason I could not participate in my Quaker meeting for a couple of months. The meeting offered a support committee, and that was helpful. I am able to attend Quaker meeting now.

But the underlying tension is still there. As I wrote yesterday, there are “lingering issues.”

This series goes deeper into those opportunities and conflicts.

# Scattergood and the Hub

*What did not reach us*

*Active Objection, 2026-06-19* · [Original post](https://activeobjection.substack.com/p/scattergood-and-the-hub)[^original-post]

I’ve been surprised by the role Scattergood Friends School and Farm is playing in my most recent work related to the Great Plains Action Society’s Indigenous-led Urban Resilience Hub in Iowa City.

I was glad to see that Scattergood offered lodging for those of us coming to work at the Hub. Sikowis Nobiss, founder of the Great Plains Action Society, had been in touch with the School before I became involved. Plans were being discussed regarding ways students could be engaged with the Hub.

Another Bear Creek meeting member, and my roommate when we attended Scattergood, Jon Tesdell, and I stayed at Scattergood during the work weeks at the Hub. We talked about our Hub work over meals at Scattergood.

While I was at the School during the first Hub work week in December, I was glad for the chance to talk to the students about the work at the Hub during a community meeting. Being at the School during subsequent work weeks offered more opportunities to talk with the students.

Jon and I had numerous informal conversations with our new friends at the Hub about Scattergood. When asked where we were staying, for example, we talked about the School. Unsurprisingly, many people at the Hub know something about the School because of the many ways it is involved in work of the wider community. Sikowis spoke about building bridges with Native peoples at Scattergood in 2017.

Scattergood prepared me for the Hub work in ways I'm only now seeing clearly.

We learned about communities of integrity through how the School ran itself. We learned about personal integrity from the examples of our teachers, and the history of Quaker work for peace and justice. We attended Quaker meetings for worship in the Hickory Grove meetinghouse on the School campus. We learned about the land from our work crews on the farm and in the orchard.

I began to see the throughlines from what I learned at Scattergood converging again.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!TlrW!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fbed37900-698e-4f53-9521-0dde22fcb35b_2760x1880.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!TlrW!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fbed37900-698e-4f53-9521-0dde22fcb35b_2760x1880.png)

There was one exception to what we were taught. That being the history of Quaker involvement in settler-colonialism, including with the Indian Boarding Schools. This is the glaring issue I’m being confronted with, and the root of my struggle with Quaker complicity in colonialism.

I call this arc “**what did not reach us**.” Instead of something like “what was hidden from us.” Because I do not believe our teachers at Scattergood were instructed to not teach us this history. I believe they didn’t know much of this history themselves.

I did not know much of this myself. I was in the class of 1970. It is ironic that Scattergood was established in 1890, at the same time Quakers were also establishing Indian boarding schools.

I only remember one conversation about this when I was a child. I was told some Quakers went to those schools to help the Native children.
