# Personal experience with Quaker Indian Boarding Schools

*More that did not reach us*

*Active Objection, 2026-06-20* · [Original post](https://activeobjection.substack.com/p/personal-experience-with-quaker-indian)[^original-post]

Yesterday I wrote about **[“what did not reach us”](https://activeobjection.substack.com/p/scattergood-and-the-hub)** regarding the Quaker involvement in the Indian Boarding Schools and my education as a student at Scattergood Friends School. I was horrified when I did begin to learn more about what happened in those institutions of forced assimilation.

One personal experience I’ve had related to the Quaker Indian Boarding School history occurred on July 22, 2024, when I was part of a traditional Arapaho ceremony in West Branch, Iowa, to remember Grace Yellowhair and help her pass over to the other side 141 years after her death and burial in West Branch Municipal Cemetery.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!K9aY!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9df621d3-56c9-481b-bf29-784225426029_1024x607.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!K9aY!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9df621d3-56c9-481b-bf29-784225426029_1024x607.png)

A remarkable series of events unfolded from a research paper by Park Ranger Peter Hoehnle, a National Park Service guide at the Herbert Hoover National Historic Site, who holds a doctorate in history. This is a link to that paper, [The West Branch Industrial School](https://bit.ly/4cMdgS5).

My friend and member of the West Branch Quaker meeting, Judy Cottingham, contacted me when she discovered Peter’s paper, because she knew of my interest and concerns related to Indigenous peoples.

I contacted my friend, Paula Palmer, whose ministry is related to Quakers and the Indian Boarding Schools. She, also, had not known about the West Branch school.

One of the many things we learned from Peter’s paper was of the deaths of two students at the school, and their burial in unmarked graves in the West Branch Municipal Cemetery.

Paula Palmer knows Frank MedicineWater who is the Cheyenne-Arapaho tribal officer trying to identify the Cheyenne and Arapaho students who attended boarding schools and trace their descendants. She sent him the article about the Quaker schools for Cheyenne and Arapaho in Indian Territory.

Frank MedicineWater must have contacted Fred Mosqueda, the Arapaho Language and Culture Program Outreach Specialist Coordinator for the Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes of Oklahoma, who wrote:

> Thank you very much for this information. I am very interested in obtaining information of the Arapaho girl, Grace Yellowhair, and the whereabouts of the cemetery. My wife was raised partially by her Grandfather, Gustave Yellowhair. I am sure I can trace lineage to Grace. Thank you again.
> **–Fred Mosqueda**

---

When we heard about this, Judy and I felt moved to do something. It didn’t matter that our yearly meeting, Iowa Yearly Meeting (Conservative), was not involved with the school, as far as we can tell. I did tell our Yearly Meeting clerk about this. Judy invited West Branch Friends Church to participate in the events.

#### Marking the gravesite

Judy continued correspondence with Fred, in particular about his desire to come to the gravesite. Judy also did research to find the unmarked plots where Grace Yellowhair and Theodore Rodgers, Osage, were buried near each other in the Friends’ section of the West Branch Municipal Cemetery. Before the gathering Monday, white flags had been placed at the site by city staff to mark their location.

This photo shows the white flags marking the location of Grace and Theodore’s graves.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!L8tE!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7839c5b3-8fe4-4a6b-8c40-0a3bf7dcc2c7_6399x3006.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!L8tE!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7839c5b3-8fe4-4a6b-8c40-0a3bf7dcc2c7_6399x3006.jpeg)

The family did not want to disinter Grace’s remains. But they felt it necessary to come to the gravesite to perform the ceremonies that would allow Grace to pass over to the other side. Since that had not been done before, her spirit could not leave. With the ceremony, her spirit was finally set free.

The ceremony was held Monday, July 22nd, at the gravesite of Grace. The Yellowhair family included Theodore Rodgers, Osage, in the prayers to assist him too in passing to the other side. The family did not want a public event. I’m very glad I was able to attend the powerful ceremony. Among the others attending were Judy and her husband Jim Cottingham, a number of members of the West Branch Friends Meeting of Iowa Yearly Meeting (Conservative), West Branch Friends Church, and guests including Peter Hoehnle, and the West Branch mayor.

Traveling from Oklahoma to attend the ceremony with Fred Mosqueda were his wife Mary Fletcher, and John Fletcher, Mary’s brother.

At the gravesite, Fred Mosqueda moved slowly through those gathered before the ceremony began, greeting each person. Cedar was burned. Feathers fanned the smoke. Fred sang three songs with his drum. We stood in silence together to witness. I strongly felt the presence of the Spirit.

Grace Yellowhair arrived at the West Branch Industrial School in March 1883. She was fifteen years old. She died in September. She waited 141 years for what happened that Monday morning in West Branch.

That is what repair looks like when it finally arrives.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!a4TR!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb5a018b2-1829-40a4-844f-f63ddc684591_7008x3205.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!a4TR!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb5a018b2-1829-40a4-844f-f63ddc684591_7008x3205.jpeg)

---

You can read more about this story from what I wrote **[Journey July 22 West Branch Industrial School](https://unflinching.blog/2024/07/29/journey-july-22-west-branch-industrial-school/)** .

---

#### West Branch Industrial School

> The boarding school movement grew from the so-called “peace policy” pursued by President Ulysses S. Grant’s administration in the 1870s. A key component of this policy, advocated by members of the Religious Society of Friends (Quakers) was Grant’s appointment of Quakers to positions of authority in Native American policy. Among the Quakers who took an active interest in Native American rights were several members of the West Branch community, particularly members of the extended Miles family. Benjamin Miles, the head of the family, was an Ohio native, who arrived in West Branch, a widower with children, in 1856. Two years after arriving, Miles married Elizabeth Bean, whose brother, Joel, became a prominent figure in the evangelical/ progressive doctrinal split of the Quakers in the 1880s. Elizabeth Miles was a graduate of the Rhode Island Friends Boarding School, and often served as a clerk in the West Branch Quaker meeting.
>
> In 1868, the Miles family moved from their farm to a home in the village of West Branch.
>
> …
>
> The school opened on January 16, 1883. In addition to Benjamin and Elizabeth Miles, the staff included teachers, Miss Jennie Crosbie, and Sina Ann Branson, who oversaw the culinary department. By arrangement with the government, Mr. and Mrs. Miles were paid $167 per year “for the keep of each Indian boy or girl sent to the school.”
>
> **Peter Hoehnle, [The West Branch Industrial School](https://bit.ly/4cMdgS5)**

---

#### Death of Grace Yellowhair

> A particularly unfortunate consequence of the boarding schools was that a significant number of the children enrolled in them succumbed to disease and died. In many cases, the students were exposed to diseases for which they had no natural immunity. In charitable schools of this type, it would also not have been uncommon for students to use the same wash water. Further, living in a converted store building, as they did, there is a high probability that sanitary systems were simply inadequate. The students at the West Branch school were no exception, unfortunately. On June 15, 1883 – A student at the school, who was approximately eight, died of “malaria fever,” and was buried in an unmarked grave in the Quaker section of the West Branch Cemetery. The West Branch Local Record reported the death: “Friday morning, June 15th, 1883, of malaria fever, after lingering several weeks, THEADORE ROGERS, aged 8 years. This little boy was a member of the Indian Industrial School at this place, bright and industrious for one of his age, cheerful though quiet in disposition. He bore up under his affliction with remarkable courage, His mother and stepfather, members of the Osage tribe reside in the Indian Territory. The funeral occurred Saturday at 10 A.M. from the Friends’ Church.”
>
> A second death, that of Grace Yellow Hair, from the Arapaho Nation, occurred on September 11, 1883 –She was fifteen years old and had suffered a lingering illness for two months. Her illness is diagnosed as malaria. She had arrived at the school in mid-March. She was buried next to Theodore Rogers in the West Branch Cemetery. Her grave, likewise, remains unmarked.
>
> (See West Branch Local Record of September 13, 1883; Bears, Buildings in the Core-Area, 269.)
>
> **Peter Hoehnle, [The West Branch Industrial School](https://bit.ly/4cMdgS5)**

# Introduction to the Hub

*Indigenous-led Urban Resilience and Innovation Hub*

*Active Objection, 2026-06-21* · [Original post](https://activeobjection.substack.com/p/introduction-to-the-hub)[^original-post]

**Relationship to the land has always been fundamental to Indigenous life.**

When I asked my friend Sikowis Nobiss how she came up with the plans for the Urban Resilience Hub, she said, like many things, it came to her in a dream. When she awoke from this dream, she looked for available properties and immediately found the 1.2 acres of land where the Great Plains Actions Society’s Indigenous-led Urban Resilience and Innovation Hub is now being built. This is at the corner of Maiden Lane and East Benton Street in downtown Iowa City. The ownership was approved by the Iowa City Council in October, 2025.

It is shocking to realize how completely Indigenous peoples have been dispossessed of their land. The Hub is one of **only three properties** that are Indigenous owned in Iowa. In 1857, the Meskwaki Nation pooled their own funds and formally purchased their first 80 acres of land along the Iowa River. And in 2022, the Johnson County Conservation Board officially donated 7 acres of land back to the Iowa Tribe.

---

> What does it look like when Indigenous Peoples reclaim urban land not as charity, but as justice? Join Great Plains Action Society (GPAS) for a groundbreaking panel on ReMatriation—the convergence of Indigenous Ways-of-Being, Traditional Ecological Knowledge, Matriarchal governance, and First Foods Renewal—transforming a 1.05-acre site in Iowa City into a **living laboratory for collective liberation.**
>
> In October 2025, **GPAS liberated seven adjoining lots** in Iowa City’s Riverfront Crossings district, launching an Indigenous-led micro-community that rejects colonial capitalism in favor of an economy built on compassion. This panel brings together experts to explore how urban resilience hubs can become ecosystems of resistance and renewal.
>
> *[ReMatriating Urban Spaces: Indigenous-Led Resilience Hubs and Land Liberation](https://actionnetwork.org/events/rematriating-urban-spaces-indigenous-led-resilience-hubs-and-land-liberation)*

---

The Urban Resilience and Innovation Hub is not an office or a meeting room. It is a set of physical spaces, each with a specific purpose, each part of a coherent vision of what Indigenous-led community resilience looks like in practice. Understanding the Hub means understanding what each of these spaces is for.

**Hub Center — 800 Maiden Lane** The main community space: multi-purpose rooms, an industrial kitchen, an art space, offices. This is where the community gathers, where organizations can meet and work, where the Hub’s programming lives. The industrial kitchen makes food-based mutual aid and entrepreneurship possible at scale.

**Urban Farm — 815 Gilbert Court** The urban farm is grounded in Indigenous Traditional Ecological Knowledge — the accumulated wisdom of thousands of years of Indigenous agriculture, plant medicine, and relationship with the land. This is not conventional urban farming. It is a reclamation of food sovereignty and a demonstration of what farming looks like when it begins from relationship with the land rather than extraction from it.

**Healing Justice House** A space for healing work — therapeutic, ceremonial, community-based. Healing justice recognizes that the harms of colonization are not only political and economic; they are embodied, spiritual, intergenerational. This space exists because the Hub understands that resilience is not only material. It is also the repair of the deep wounds that colonization inflicted on bodies, families, and communities.

**Launch Pads — Entrepreneurial Incubators** Spaces for Indigenous entrepreneurs to develop and grow businesses rooted in Indigenous values and knowledge systems. Indigenous entrepreneurship on Indigenous terms — not assimilation into the extractive economy, but building economic power within a different framework.

**Mutual Aid Café — 410 E Benton Street** A coffee shop operating on the mutual aid model: food available to anyone who comes, no eligibility rules, no sorting of people into deserving and undeserving. This model was pioneered by the Black Panthers in the 1960s and has been continued by mutual aid organizations across the country. The café is not a charity project. **It is a material refusal of the economy that sorts people, and a demonstration that a different kind of economy is possible.**

---

# Children as hostages

*Active Objection, 2026-07-07* · [Original post](https://activeobjection.substack.com/p/children-as-hostages)[^original-post]

***The use of Native children as hostages is the most despicable aspect of the settler-colonization of this land.***

**[Writing about Grace Yellowhair yesterday](https://activeobjection.substack.com/p/my-example-of-how-it-reached-us)** brings back the devastation, sorrow, and anger I felt when I attended her ceremony at the West Branch, Iowa, cemetery two years ago.

Can you even imagine having government agents appear in your home to forcibly take your children away? One account I read told of the complete silence in the community after children had been taken.

International law explicitly recognizes that removing a people’s children is a mechanism of genocide. The 1948 UN Convention on Genocide, Article II(e), lists **“forcibly transferring children of the group to another group”** among the acts constituting genocide.

Captain Richard Henry Pratt opened the Carlisle Indian Industrial School in 1879. The War Department sent Pratt to the Oglala leader Red Cloud and the Sicangu leader Spotted Tail to compel them to give up their children, with the acknowledged aim of gaining leverage over the tribes amid the continuing effort to take their land. Pratt’s own words: **“The children would be hostages for the good behavior of the people.”**

The system’s intent was never educational; it was extractive. The Interior Department’s Federal Indian Boarding School Initiative Investigative Report (updated in 2024) confirms that the United States **“directly targeted American Indian, Alaska Native, and Native Hawaiian children in the pursuit of a policy of cultural assimilation that coincided with Indian territorial dispossession.”**

Across the border, the objective was identical. Duncan Campbell Scott, the official who ran Canada’s residential schools, told a 1920 parliamentary committee: **“Our object is to continue until there is not a single Indian in Canada that has not been absorbed into the body politic, and there is no Indian question, and no Indian department.”**

The devastation of these policies is still being uncovered. As noted by the Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Canada, **at least 3,200 children died at Canadian residential schools**—often from tuberculosis, malnutrition, and neglect—though the real number is likely far higher.

---

#### Quaker apology

Today, the focus has shifted toward repatriation, rematriation, truth-telling, and institutional accountability.

This history requires a reckoning from the institutions that participated in it. Writing in *Friends Journal* in early 2026, Quaker authors Paula Palmer and Paula Keeth documented their formal apology to Arapaho and Cheyenne families:

> “More children will come home to us,” Mosqueda told us. “We are looking for them, and we will care for them.” **Another Arapaho child who died while attending a Quaker-operated Indian boarding school in West Branch, Iowa,** remains in a cemetery there after Fred and Mary Mosqueda visited and prayed at the gravesite in 2024. “She will be safe there,” Mosqueda said.
>
> ---
>
> When we were called to speak, we read from a letter we had sent in advance to Arapaho and Cheyenne families and tribal officers. In part, it read:
>
> *We grieve the deaths of these children, knowing that the actions of our Quaker forebears are at least in part responsible. We are deeply sorry for the harms and losses the Arapaho and Cheyenne people have suffered. Feeling this remorse, we humbly hope to build new relationships with the tribes, based on truth, respect, justice, and our shared humanity. In this spirit, we are with you here today.*
>
> **Personal Reflections**
>
> *Paula Palmer: We were wearing dresses out of respect, although dresses are unusual attire for both of us. Maybe that made it easier for me to feel present there as a nineteenth-century Friend and also as myself at this moment in time. It felt important to bridge the 155 years of shared history among the Arapaho, Cheyenne, and Quakers. Through our research, we have learned who Quakers were then, and how their actions have reverberated through centuries. Now we ask: **Who are Quakers today? What actions are we taking now, and how will they reverberate into the future?***
>
> [A Homecoming for the Arapaho and Cheyenne](https://www.friendsjournal.org/a-homecoming-for-the-arapaho-and-cheyenne/) By Paula Palmer and Paula Keeth, Friends Journal, January 1, 2026

# Why don’t we bring them home?

*Sicangu Youth Council*

*Active Objection, 2026-07-08* · [Original post](https://activeobjection.substack.com/p/why-dont-we-bring-them-home)[^original-post]

The stories about the Indian boarding schools and forced assimilation are very difficult to hear. They are at the root of an answer to “**what did not reach us?**” “Us” referring to non-Native peoples.

It’s important for non-Native people to hear directly from Indigenous voices. Especially important to learn how this continues to affect Native people today. In the powerful video below Amy Goodman of **Democracy Now** interviews **Sicangu Youth Council** member Christopher Eagle Bear. Thanks to the work of the Sicangu Youth Council, the U.S. Army agreed to disinter and return the remains of nine Lakota children who had died over 140 years ago at the Carlisle Indian Industrial School in Pennsylvania.

[Embedded content](https://www.youtube-nocookie.com/embed/PWfzCgDh28c?rel=0&autoplay=0&showinfo=0&enablejsapi=0)

---

This National Geographic article is about the journey of returning the children home.

**[These Indigenous children died far away more than a century ago. Here’s how they finally got home.](https://www.nationalgeographic.com/history/article/these-indigenous-children-died-far-away-more-than-a-century-ago-heres-how-they-finally-got-home)**

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!4QzI!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F52e1a758-181f-45e2-8d6a-3656dfd6f3f5_1768x872.png)](https://www.nationalgeographic.com/history/article/these-indigenous-children-died-far-away-more-than-a-century-ago-heres-how-they-finally-got-home)

---

#### July 2021 Great Plains Action Society

The Great Plains Action Society (GPAS) organized an event in Sioux City to welcome these children on their journey home, as explained below. This speaks to the depth of the organizing Great Plains has been doing for years. My friend Sikowis Nobiss is the founder and Executive Director of GPAS.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!7TI7!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff4aff9f3-9ebd-47de-8021-62729eb60cc1_700x272.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!7TI7!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff4aff9f3-9ebd-47de-8021-62729eb60cc1_700x272.png)

> On July 15-16, we organized and hosted an event in Sioux City to welcome the return of nine children from Carlisle Indian Boarding School back to the Sicangu Oyate Nation (Rosebud Nation) as they passed through. We hosted a community meal and prayer on the 15th for 415 folks and served traditional foods. There were family members of the children in attendance and we were honored to offer them some support. In the evening the large caravan carrying the children arrived and we lit a fire in a tipi set up with nine seats, toys and blankets. This event was held at War Eagle Park in Sioux City Iowa, **a place that local Natives are taking back**.
>
> Great Plains Action Society spent over $4,000 to set up and host this one event, and there are more than 480 residential schools in the US and Canada that have not been searched. Our work has just begun.
>
> — ***Sikowis Nobiss, Great Plains Action Society***

Nine seats. Nine sets of toys. Nine blankets. That kind of readiness doesn't happen without years of work.
